definition: A comparison of two versions of something, shown at random to different people, measuring which produces a better outcome on a metric chosen in advance.
Analysis carried out by an AI agent in steps — planning, querying, reading the result and revising — rather than in a single pass.
Collapsing many rows into a summary value — a count, sum, average or percentile — usually grouped by one or more columns.
A rule that watches a saved question and notifies people by email or chat when its result crosses a condition.
A database organised for scanning and summarising large volumes of rows, as opposed to a transactional database optimised for reading and writing individual records.
A defined set of endpoints one program exposes so other programs can read from it or act on it.
The database an analytics tool keeps its own configuration in — questions, dashboards, users — as opposed to the data it reports on.
A line chart with the space beneath the line filled, used to show how a total is composed over time.
Annual recurring revenue: the yearly value of subscriptions currently active, usually monthly recurring revenue times twelve.
A property carried on a record or a user, often used to decide what that person is allowed to see.
A record of who did what and when, used to answer questions about access and change after the fact.
A chart comparing values across categories using bars whose lengths are proportional to the numbers.
Software for exploring data and publishing the results, so people can answer questions without writing code.
One bucket of a continuous range, used to turn values like ages or prices into countable groups.
Splitting an aggregate by the values of another column, so one number becomes one number per group.
A scatter plot where each point is sized by a third value, letting three dimensions share one view.
The practice of turning operational data into answers that inform decisions, covering the tooling, the modelling and the conventions a team agrees on.
Customer acquisition cost: total sales and marketing spend divided by the number of customers it won.
One tile on a dashboard: a chart, a number, a table or a block of text.
The number of distinct values in a column. High-cardinality columns such as user IDs behave very differently in grouping and indexing than low-cardinality ones such as country.
Streaming the inserts, updates and deletes made to a source database so another system can stay in step with it.
The share of customers or revenue lost over a period, the counterpart to growth.
A SQL function returning the first value in its arguments that is not null, used to supply a fallback.
Grouping records by when they first appeared and tracking each group separately over time, so that changes in behaviour are not hidden by changes in mix.
A folder holding questions, dashboards and models, and the unit permissions are usually granted on.
One field of a table, holding the same kind of value for every row.
Storing a table column by column rather than row by row, so a query that reads a few columns of many rows touches far less data.
A chart mixing bars and lines on shared axes, usually to show a count and a rate together.
Merging many small files or segments into fewer larger ones so later reads are cheaper.
A function joining several strings end to end into one.
A set of user-experience measurements — loading, interactivity and visual stability — used to judge how a page performs for real visitors.
Clicking part of one chart to filter the rest of the dashboard by what you clicked.
A named result set defined at the top of a SQL query with WITH, so a later part of the query can read it like a table.
A chart plotting a running total, so each point includes everything before it.
A column computed from other columns at query time rather than stored in the table.
A click behaviour that sends someone from a chart to a chosen dashboard, question or URL.
A formula written in a query builder to compute, filter or aggregate without dropping into SQL.
A directed acyclic graph: a set of steps with dependencies and no cycles, the usual shape of a data pipeline.
A collection of visualisations and filters presented together, ideally answering one question rather than displaying everything available.
A schedule that sends a dashboard's current results to people by email or chat.
An agreement about a dataset's shape, meaning and guarantees, so consumers can rely on it and producers know what they may not break.
A catalogue describing each table and column in plain language, so people know what a field actually means.
Cheap storage holding raw files in many formats, queried where they lie rather than loaded first.
A lake with a table layer over it, bringing transactions and schema to files kept in open formats.
The record of where a value came from — which source tables, transformations and definitions produced it — used to trace errors and assess trust.
A subset of a warehouse shaped for one team or subject, so its questions are quick to ask.
An approach where domain teams own and publish their own data as products, rather than a central team owning everything.
The agreed structure of tables and relationships, and the meaning attached to them.
The sequence of moves and transformations carrying data from where it is produced to where it is analysed.
Built-in documentation of the tables and fields a tool can see, read while you work.
A rule restricting someone to a slice of a table, so the same question returns only their rows.
What kind of value a column holds — text, number, date, boolean — which decides how it can be used.
A database built for analysis, holding data brought together from several systems and organised for querying rather than transactions.
A lookup structure making some queries much faster to run, at the cost of space and slower writes.
A column you group or slice by, such as country or plan, as opposed to the number being measured.
Clicking an element of a chart to see the underlying records or a more granular breakdown, rather than writing a new query.
Analytics presented inside another application, so that a product's own users see reporting about their own data without leaving it.
Putting charts or dashboards inside another product so its users never leave it to see their data.
The column identifying what a row is about, used to join it to other tables.
An entity relationship diagram: a picture of tables and how they key into one another.
Extract, transform, load. Moving data from source systems into an analytical store, reshaping it on the way.
The row multiplication that happens when joining across a one-to-many relationship, silently inflating sums and counts if unnoticed.
Another name for a column: one named piece of each record.
A SQL variable mapped to a real column, so a filter widget can drive it with the right type and values.
An expression deriving a new field from existing ones.
The semantic role a column plays — a city, a price, a creation timestamp — as distinct from the data type that says how it is stored.
A condition narrowing a result to the rows that satisfy it.
The control on a dashboard that lets a reader change a filter without editing anything.
A column pointing at another table's key, which is what makes a join meaningful.
A join keeping every row from both tables, filling the gaps with nulls where there is no match.
A chart showing how many people remain at each step of a sequence, and where they drop out.
A dial showing a single value against bands of good and bad.
An open format describing geographic shapes, used to draw custom map regions.
A reference line drawn across a chart at a target value.
The level of detail one row represents — a single event, a daily total, a monthly summary. Mixing granularities in one calculation is a common source of wrong numbers.
A map dividing an area into cells and shading each by the value in it.
The SQL clause collapsing rows into one row per distinct combination of the listed columns.
A question assembled in a visual editor rather than written as SQL.
The SQL clause filtering on the result of an aggregate, after grouping rather than before.
A grid where colour carries the value, used to show where the extremes sit.
A bar chart of how often values fall into each bin, showing a distribution rather than a comparison.
Handling more load by adding more machines rather than making one machine bigger.
A join keeping only rows that match on both sides.
Combining rows from two tables by matching on a shared key.
A text format for nested data, widely used by APIs and for semi-structured columns.
A signed token carrying claims about a user, commonly used to authenticate an embedded session.
A key performance indicator: the small number of measures an organisation agrees to steer by.
A directory protocol many organisations use to hold accounts and groups centrally.
A measure that moves before the outcome you care about, giving you time to act.
A join keeping every row from the left table, with nulls where the right has no match.
A chart joining points in order, used to show how a value moves over time.
An axis where equal distances represent equal differences in value.
A dashboard filter whose options are narrowed by another filter's current selection.
A component spreading incoming requests across several servers.
A stored result of a query, refreshed on a schedule, traded against freshness to avoid recomputing something expensive on every request.
A reusable, named calculation — revenue, active users — defined once so every chart counts it the same way.
A convention of layering a warehouse into raw, cleaned and curated stages, often called bronze, silver and gold.
Data describing other data: names, types, descriptions, lineage and ownership.
A named, agreed calculation such as active users or net revenue. The value of a metric is less in the arithmetic than in everyone using the same one.
A saved, curated starting point built on top of raw tables, so people explore from something already cleaned up.
An open protocol letting an AI assistant discover and call external tools and data sources in a uniform way.
Serving many customers from one system while keeping each customer's data strictly separate, usually enforced at the data layer rather than in application code.
One deployment serving many customers, with each one's data kept separate from the others'.
A query written in the database's own language rather than assembled in a builder.
The editor for writing SQL directly, with the schema to hand.
Structuring tables so each fact is stored once, reducing contradiction at the cost of more joins when querying.
The single measure a team agrees best captures the value it delivers.
A step-by-step visual editor where joins, filters and summaries stack as readable blocks.
Online analytical processing. Query patterns that scan and aggregate many rows to answer questions about trends, as opposed to retrieving individual records.
Online transaction processing: a database tuned for many small reads and writes, which is what applications need and analysis does not.
An axis treating values as ordered categories, spacing them evenly regardless of distance.
The top-level collection everything else is nested inside.
A placeholder in a query whose value is supplied when it runs.
A private space only its owner and administrators can see.
A circle divided into slices by share of a total, legible only when there are few categories.
A map placing a marker at each row's coordinates.
A table summarising values across two axes at once, with groups down the side and across the top.
An expression evaluating to true or false, used to decide which rows qualify.
The column uniquely identifying each row of a table.
The live database an application runs on, where heavy analytical queries are usually unwelcome.
Sharing a chart or dashboard by URL without requiring the viewer to sign in.
A scheduled delivery of results to a channel or inbox.
A visual interface for assembling a query by choosing data, filters and summaries.
A saved query together with how its answer should be displayed.
Retrieval-augmented generation: fetching relevant documents and giving them to a language model so its answer is grounded in them.
A copy of a database kept in step with the original and used for reads, keeping load off the primary.
One row: a single instance of whatever the table describes.
A map shading predefined areas such as countries or states by value.
A database storing data in tables of rows and columns, with keys expressing how they relate.
The share of customers still active after a given period, the complement of churn.
Pushing modelled data back out of the warehouse into the tools teams work in.
A join keeping every row from the right table, with nulls where the left has no match.
One entry in a table, holding a value for each column.
A bar chart drawn horizontally, which suits long category labels.
Restricting which rows a person can see based on their identity, applied by the data layer so that every query is filtered regardless of how it was written.
A standard for passing authentication between an identity provider and an application.
A small bundled dataset for learning and demonstration.
A flow diagram where the width of each path shows the quantity moving along it.
A question kept for reuse, which other questions and dashboards can build on.
A chart plotting two numeric values against each other to show how they relate.
The organisation of a database: its tables, columns, types and relationships.
A filter offering matching values as you type rather than a fixed list.
The dashboard control backing a search filter.
An embed whose parameters are signed, so the host application decides what each viewer may see.
A named, reusable filter capturing a subset everyone agrees on, such as active customers.
An arrangement where people answer their own data questions, requiring both accessible tooling and a modelled, documented foundation to be safe.
The layer where raw tables are given business meaning — canonical sources, named metrics, agreed joins — so people and agents query definitions rather than raw columns.
Exporting configuration to files so it can be version-controlled and moved between instances.
A measure derived from a single visit rather than from a person over time.
A short-lived credential identifying an authenticated session.
A stock keeping unit: the identifier for one distinct sellable item.
An attribute that changes over time, such as a customer's plan, where historical accuracy requires storing the value as it was rather than only as it is now.
Marking a row as deleted rather than removing it, so history survives.
The language used to query and manipulate relational databases.
A reusable fragment of SQL that can be referenced from several queries.
Single sign-on: authenticating once with a central provider and reaching every connected application.
A bar chart where each bar is divided into parts, showing both the total and its composition.
A warehouse layout with one fact table referencing several dimension tables.
A routine held in the database and run by name.
A query nested inside another, supplying rows or a value to the outer one.
A table of pre-aggregated results, kept so common questions do not rescan the detail.
A set of rows sharing the same columns.
A dashboard tile holding written content rather than a chart.
Turning a question written in plain language into a SQL query.
A sequence of values recorded in time order.
A database tuned for the many small reads and writes an application makes.
A write that updates a row if it exists and inserts it if it does not.
A named placeholder in a query whose value is supplied at run time.
A database storing embeddings and retrieving them by similarity rather than by exact match.
A numeric representation of text or an image, positioned so that similar things sit close together.
Handling more load by giving one machine more CPU or memory.
A saved query the database presents as if it were a table.
A chart showing how a starting value reaches an ending one through successive increases and decreases.
Restyling an embedded product so it carries the host's branding rather than the vendor's.
A calculation across a set of rows related to the current row — running totals, rankings, period-over-period comparisons — without collapsing the result.
An automatically generated set of charts offering a first look at a table or a record.
